Bird Flu 2023

By: Julian Sun | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We reveal the devastating impact of bird flu on livlihoods around SA

Unique Selling Point:
We get up close and personal with people impacted and affected by the Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) that has decimated the SA Poultry Industry.

Summary:
The SA poultry industry is amid an existential crisis, as the worst outbreak of Avian Influenza in SA's history wreaks havoc on the local poultry industry. The culling of 7.2 million birds has resulted in unprecedented egg and chicken shortages, posing a real danger to food security in South Africa. With the outbreak far from being contained, the government has been forced to import eggs and meat to mitigate against shortages this festive season but the impact of HPAI will linger longer.

It's estimated that it will take the industry 18 months to recover. As farms continue to face losses and uncertainty, the jobs of about 110,000 people
employed by the poultry industry remain at risk.

Further information:
We provide a human face to the impact of bird flu

We meet Beverly Mhlabane, an independent egg producer who had the world at her feet at the beginning of the year. But in August, bird flu wiped out her entire flock of 10000 birds, and now faces bankruptcy

Then we see the tragedy that's unfolding through the eyes of Obed Lukhele vet with Astral Foods - the largest chicken producer in the country. He and his team have had to cull thousands of birds. We reveal the emotional toll it's taken

Finally, we meet free-range farmer Leanne Dirkson. While her farm is free from bird flu, she fears that an outbreak would wipe her out.

Press Release:


A deadly outbreak of avian flu has left South Africa’s poultry industry on the brink of disaster. With millions of chickens being culled, grocery stores are forced to ration meat and egg sales while the government imports eggs and meat to mitigate shortages over the festive season. But there is more than Christmas dinner at stake: some experts say the impact of the virus has been so devastating, it will take the industry 18 months to recover. And there’s a human face to the crisis, with thousands of jobs on the line, and some smaller independent suppliers facing financial ruin.

Script:


BIRD FLU SCRIPT

VIZ: Lourensa walking with egg farmer Bev Mahlabane on her farm; walk toward a concrete slab - the final resting place for 8,000 chickens

Beverly: It was around the 17th of August. And walked into the into the house and they're like 150 roughly birds dead…

Beverly: When the chickens started dying, um, the vet state vet actually saw this area and then said, we can bury them here.

Lourensa: So how many chickens did you have to bury here?

Beverly: Uh, over 6000. 8000.

Lourensa: So what do you feel when you stand here and look at the site?

Beverly: That's my livelihood gone dreams. Yeah. Um, people don't have work now because it's gone. Within a few days. Yeah. What can I do?

Fade to black

LOURENSA: I’m on a farm in Benoni on the East Rand. It was once home to 10,000 healthy egg-producing chickens until August this year. That’s when it was hit by a highly pathogenic strain of avian influenza. Within days, thousands of birds were dead and the rest had to be culled. Now not one bird is left and a once-thriving business is destroyed.

Establish Bev using portrait shots

V/O: Beverly Mahlabane is a chemical engineer who left a secure corporate job to explore her passion for farming.

We pick up with Bev and Lourensa walking into an empty chicken house

Bev: I had no prior experience with farming, I'm a Google farmer. I started with ten chickens literally in my backyard. And the idea was just to feed my family and ten chickens went to 100 chickens. And I took a neighbour who actually showed me that it could be a business. And that's how I started.

V/O: Within a decade, Beverly was turning over millions of rands annually.
She was thriving.

Cut to Bev on her Tuk Tuk

V/O: Then in August bird flu began infecting neighbouring farms in her area.

Beverly: That day as I walked in, I got a report that there’s a lot of dead chickens. I immediately called the state vet to come and check what was wrong. They confirmed it was Avian Flu and basically had to cull everything else that was left.

V/O: Beverly is one of 112 farmers affected by the worst outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza in South African history that has brought the industry to its knees.

Izaak Breitenbach is from the South African Poultry Association.

Izaak: The consequence of the disease is dire. And we had phone calls of very emotional farmers at the brink of losing everything they've got. Every single morning, we will wake up with new farms being diagnosed with the disease. That was like a veld fire.

V/O: Just like COVID-19, Avian Influenza is a viral disease
Previous outbreaks were due to the H5N1 strain - which hit coastal farms in March.

V/O: Then in May things deteriorated when a new virulent strain called H7N6 began spreading through the densely populated farms of Gauteng.

V/O: H7 is a silent killer that infects chickens long before they show symptoms. This incubation period can last up to 2 weeks …. And all this time, the infected birds shed the virus. That’s the reason for the uncontrollable spread that’s decimated farms in the region.

Izaak: Normally we could contain the disease, but this time around we believe that it might be windborne or dust-bourne. Farmers actually did a lot in terms of biosecurity and they still couldn't contain the disease.

V/O: Astral is the largest chicken producer in the country. On one of their farms in Standerton, Mpumalanga they showed us the extreme lengths they go to, to prevent disease-causing germs from entering or leaving their facility.
These are standard biosecurity protocols they practice - every day.

Montage of Lourensa going through biosecurity at Astral

Lourensa: This virus is highly contagious. When we arrived here, I had to get undressed. I left my private clothes in the restroom. I got dressed in red overalls whereafter I had to take a full shower. And then I got dressed in these blue overalls. And despite these stringent biosecurity measures, the virus still managed to make its way onto the facility.

V/O: Once Avian Influenza is detected, there’s no way out: all the birds in an infected chicken house must be culled.

It’s a grim task that still haunts Astral’s Group Vet Obed Lukhele.

Obed and Lourensa walk through the empty chicken house

Lourensa: What do you feel like now walking through here and seeing this place so lifeless?

Obed: In my almost 17 years working with chickens. I've never experienced this. It's completely unusual. But it is also devastating. … You wake up one day, you have to cull those birds and, it is not mentally good for us. You really break down and cry because you feel very helpless and I do not want to do that again in my life.

V/O: The disease also threatens the local economy - Astral is one of the biggest employers in Standerton. Apart from the farm, they also run a processing plant. The scale of production is massive – and many jobs hang in the balance because of this epidemic.

Montage of Lourensa touring processing plant.

V/O: To make matters worse, independent farmers face financial ruin, because there is no safety net - like elsewhere in the world, where farmers are compensated for birds they cull. Legally, it should be happening in South Africa too, but it’s not.

Izaak: [00:22:55] The Department of Agriculture specifically said that they do not have the money to reimburse farmers. and the farmers are really left to its own devices

Beverly: [00:15:16] To fill up my two houses, I need over a million rands. And I don't have money like that lying around. So without government compensation, there's no way that I can start.

Some years ago, the government celebrated Beverly for her entrepreneurial success … but now, in her time of need…

Lourensa: [00:18:50] But you were mentioned in a budget speech by Minister Ebrahim Patel

Beverly: [00:18:53] Yes. I actually thought maybe they'll come back quickly. He did. But I was hoping that they would come back quickly and assist us. But I haven't heard anything from anybody.

Lourensa: [00:19:06] So you're good enough to brag about that when you need help. There's no sign of.

Beverly: [00:19:11] No.

PAUSE AND VISUALLY SEGUE AWAY FROM BEVERLY

In the meantime, Government announced they’re looking into a relief package for affected farmers …the details are yet to be provided.

Izaak: But this is not about the farmers. This is about food security for the people of South Africa.

V/O: With over 10 million birds lost so far, South Africans’s staple protein has become scarcer and pricier.

V/O: While the rate of infection has declined, that’s because there are no more birds left to infect. Many farms stand empty and the outbreak is far from over

Themba Mathebula - Astral’s breeder manager, responsible for dozens of farms in the region, is waiting… on tenterhooks … for the only thing that can turn the tide - a vaccine.

Themba: [00:14:08] There are farms where they repopulated, then they still get affected. So you see as and then it's double loss. So rather safeguard by doing what? Bring the vaccine, vaccinate, put the birds on the floor. Then you know for sure you're not going to be by the same strain again. That would be much, much better.

Lourensa: Walking through this empty chicken house is sad and eerie and the only way to bring it back to life is to vaccinate but it remains to be seen if this happens sooner rather than later.

V/O: While vaccines exist for the older H5 strain, one for H7 must still be developed and just like COVID, must undergo rigorous testing before being approved for use in South Africa…a long process.

Izaak: [00:29:19] It'll take about between two and six months before we will have the vaccine available. Unfortunately, it will not be available for this outbreak that we currently experienced, but certainly, it will help us prevent us getting into the same situation that we are now.

V/O: … that’s 6 more months of fear and uncertainty and even if the outbreak is contained - another 18 months for the industry to recover.

Yet the one person who has every right to be cynical still has faith.

Beverly: [00:00:25] It will happen. The vaccines will will will be approved, I believe, and and will come back into production. I mean, other countries are actually vaccinating and they are producing. So it should happen in South Africa as well? It should happen. It must

Lourensa: [00:23:27] Do you think that if we don't get the vaccine approved, where will you be this time next year?

Beverly: [00:23:38] I probably will go back to starting with a few chickens and I’ll fill up one chicken at a time because I cannot let the thing go down. And this is a passion for me. It's no longer a job. It's a passion. And somebody needs to pay school fees. For us to, you know, to to to make sure that we have food secure in the country. And if I don't do it, who will do it?


















PROMOS:

PROMO 1: it’s been called the worst outbreak of bird flu in South Africa and has already resulted in the loss of over 10 million chickens
The biggest problem that we're going to face is… Only people with money that can afford to buy chicken. And what's going to happen to communities?

What will the loss of so many birds mean for food security in South Africa?

PROMO 2: A new strain of Bird Flu is devastating chicken farms across South Africa and no vaccine exists for it yet.
UPS: Without a vaccine, we might not have a poultry industry this time next year.
What does the future hold for farmers who have been brought to their knees?

PROMO 3: A deadly outbreak of bird flu has laid waste to millions of chickens across South Africa.
Beverly: That's my livelihood gone dreams gone. Within a few days. Yeah. What can I do?

Without a vaccine, how will farmers pick up the pieces of their shattered lives?

metadata.Unique Selling Point: We get up close and personal with people impacted and affected by the Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) that has decimated the SA Poultry Industry.
metadata.Summary: The SA poultry industry is amid an existential crisis, as the worst outbreak of Avian Influenza in SA's history wreaks havoc on the local poultry industry. The culling of 7.2 million birds has resulted in unprecedented egg and chicken shortages, posing a real danger to food security in South Africa. With the outbreak far from being contained, the government has been forced to import eggs and meat to mitigate against shortages this festive season but the impact of HPAI will linger longer. It's estimated that it will take the industry 18 months to recover. As farms continue to face losses and uncertainty, the jobs of about 110,000 people employed by the poultry industry remain at risk.
metadata.Further information: We provide a human face to the impact of bird flu We meet Beverly Mhlabane, an independent egg producer who had the world at her feet at the beginning of the year. But in August, bird flu wiped out her entire flock of 10000 birds, and now faces bankruptcy Then we see the tragedy that's unfolding through the eyes of Obed Lukhele vet with Astral Foods - the largest chicken producer in the country. He and his team have had to cull thousands of birds. We reveal the emotional toll it's taken Finally, we meet free-range farmer Leanne Dirkson. While her farm is free from bird flu, she fears that an outbreak would wipe her out.
